summary: Help 11–13 year-olds understand that muscles can only PULL (contract), never push, which is exactly why the body needs antagonistic pairs: one muscle contracts to move a bone one way while its partner relaxes, then the partner contracts to move it back. Use the biceps/triceps at the elbow as the worked example, tracking BOTH muscles' states through bending and straightening, then generalise to a second pair such as quadriceps/hamstrings at the knee. The decisive insight is that 'muscles work in pairs' is a direct consequence of pull-only action, not an arbitrary fact to memorise.
misconceptions: Thinking muscles can push as well as pull.
Believing only one muscle (the biceps) works to both bend and straighten the arm.
Thinking both muscles of a pair contract at the same time.
Assuming a relaxed muscle actively pushes the bone back (it is pulled back by its antagonist).
Not recognising other antagonistic pairs beyond biceps/triceps.

activities.title: Bend and straighten a controllable arm
steps: Drag the forearm up and down (or use a flex/extend control) on a model elbow and watch what happens to the biceps and triceps.
Observe that as the forearm rises, the biceps shortens and bulges (contracted) while the triceps lengthens (relaxed); as the model actively straightens the arm, the two swap.
Read the colour-coding that marks each muscle as contracted or relaxed so the reciprocal swap is unmistakable.
Try to straighten the arm when given control of ONLY the biceps — discover you cannot, because a muscle can pull but not push.
Call in the triceps to pull the arm straight, then explain in your own words why two opposing muscles are needed.
Repeat with a second joint (the knee, with quadriceps and hamstrings) and state which muscle contracts for each movement.
activities.insight: Because a muscle can only pull (contract), a single muscle cannot reverse a movement; the body needs an antagonistic pair where one contracts while the partner relaxes, and the roles swap to move the bone back. This rule generalises beyond the biceps/triceps.

activities.title: Feel your own muscles take turns (predict, then test)
steps: Rest one hand across your biceps and triceps while your arm is bent.
Predict first: which muscle will tighten as you slowly straighten your arm, and why?

Slowly straighten the arm against resistance (for example, press your palm down firmly on a table, or straighten your arm while it is raised above your head so the forearm lifts against gravity) and feel which muscle hardens (contracts) and which softens (relaxes). If you just let your forearm drop downwards, gravity does much of the work and the biceps may stay firm as it controls the fall, so use resistance for a clear test.
Compare what you felt with your prediction and explain any surprise.
Answer: when the triceps contracts to straighten your arm, what is the biceps doing at that moment?
Answer: what would happen at the elbow if both muscles contracted hard at the same time?
activities.insight: Making the biceps/triceps swap embodied — predicting then feeling the triceps harden while the biceps softens as the arm is straightened against resistance — confronts the belief that a muscle 'pushes' the arm straight and shows that, to produce movement, one muscle in the pair contracts while the other relaxes.

activities.title: Name the states and transfer the rule
steps: State which muscle contracts and which relaxes when the arm is bent, and again when it is straightened.
Decide whether a muscle can push as well as pull, and justify the answer.
Name a second antagonistic pair in the body (for example quadriceps/hamstrings at the knee) and say which movement each muscle produces.
Explain in one or two sentences why pull-only muscles force the body to use muscles in pairs.
activities.insight: Consolidate the naming/state layer (which muscle is contracted/relaxed in each position) and confirm the learner can transfer the antagonistic-pair rule to a new joint and articulate the underlying cause.

checkQuestion: You bend your arm by contracting your biceps. To straighten it again, the triceps contracts and pulls. Why do you need two separate muscles here — why can't the biceps just push the arm straight again by itself?
checkAnswer: Muscles can only pull (contract), never push. So the biceps can pull the arm into a bend but cannot push it straight; a second muscle, the triceps, must pull it back the other way. As one contracts, its partner relaxes — an antagonistic pair.
